messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Shopowner
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajiv, a 29-year-old South Asian man, has been struggling with the aftermath of physical abuse by his romantic partner. He runs a small shop in a bustling neighborhood, and the daily hustle should have brought him some sense of normalcy, but instead it amplifies his anxiety. The traumatic event itself was brutal and sudden. One evening, as Rajiv was closing up his shop, his partner showed up unexpectedly, fueled by rage and alcohol. The assault was swift, with blows that left Rajiv dazed and bruised. The smell of sweat and body odor mixed with the overwhelming fear and helplessness he felt during the attack. Since then, any whiff of sweat or strong body odors triggers a wave of panic and intrusive memories. Rajiv had come to believe that his body was his enemy, continually reacting as if danger lurked around every corner. He would often find himself hypervigilant, especially at night when the world seemed more menacing. The darkness intensified his sense of vulnerability, making it nearly impossible for him to feel safe until dawn broke. The assault had left Rajiv with a deep-seated guilt that he could not shake off. He was certain that if only he had reacted differently or done something more, perhaps he could have prevented the abuse. This constant self-blame exacerbated his feelings of helplessness and made it difficult for him to trust himself in similar situations. His shop, which used to be a source of pride and solace, now became a place where triggers lurked around every corner. Certain conversation topics with customers or vendors could unexpectedly bring back the full memory of the event, leaving Rajiv feeling overwhelmed and on edge. He found himself avoiding conversations about relationships or past experiences, isolating himself from social interactions that once felt natural. The intrusion of memories also affected his ability to concentrate. At times, intense rage would surge through him when he recalled the abuse, making it challenging to focus on tasks at hand. Other moments were marked by an overwhelming emotional intensity without a clear memory, leaving Rajiv feeling raw and exposed. Rajiv’s sleep problems began shortly after the assault. He found himself constantly waking up in the middle of the night, bathed in sweat and drenched with fear. The lack of rest only compounded his irritability and difficulty managing daily stressors. His relationship suffered as a result; he and his partner now communicated less frequently and avoided discussing personal matters altogether. The cumulative effect of these symptoms was profound. Rajiv’s business began to suffer due to his frequent absences and reduced engagement with customers. He felt like a shadow of the man he once was, someone who could no longer rely on himself in critical moments. His partner noticed the changes but often attributed them to work stress, leaving Rajiv feeling misunderstood and isolated. What finally brought Rajiv to seek help was an incident at his shop where a customer, approaching him with the usual friendly chatter, triggered a wave of panic and rage. He reacted sharply, causing a scene that left both him and the customer shaken. This episode highlighted for Rajiv how deeply his trauma affected not just himself but those around him. Rajiv is now most afraid that he will continue to spiral downward, unable to break free from the cycle of fear and guilt. Yet, he also holds onto hope that with help, he can regain a sense of control over his life and find peace in both his personal and professional worlds.
